q-idiom-meaning.label: Meaning of an idiom
q-idiom-meaning.summary: An idiom in inverted commas; pick the option that gives its meaning.

q-idiom-identify.label: Pick the idiom that has this meaning
q-idiom-identify.summary: A meaning is spelled out in full; pick the idiom (from four real idioms) that actually means that.

rules.text: An idiom means something different from its words put together. Never choose the option that restates the literal picture.
rules.ok: Spill the beans = reveal a secret.
rules.bad: Spill the beans = drop some beans.

rules.text: Idioms cluster by feeling: trouble, anger, secrecy, ease, effort, luck, haste. Decide the feeling from the sentence, then match the option with that feeling.
rules.ok: 'in hot water' and 'on thin ice' both say trouble or risk.
rules.bad: Choosing an effort meaning for 'in hot water'.

rules.text: When the meaning is given and the idiom itself is the answer, the three wrong options are usually other real idioms, often built from the same image or word (bell, blood, water). Match the feeling of the given meaning first, then confirm by recalling the exact idiom; do not pick an option merely because it shares a word with the meaning.
rules.bad: Picking 'sound as a bell' because it also contains 'bell'.

q-idiom-meaning.cue: 'Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom/phrase' with the idiom in inverted commas. Four to five per paper in total; three appeared in the three 12 Sep 2025 papers.
q-idiom-meaning.standard: Recall the meaning as a unit, then match it. If you do not know it, work out the feeling the idiom carries (good, bad, secret, effort, anger) from the sentence it came from.
q-idiom-meaning.fast: Drop any option that is the literal reading, then match the remaining ones by feeling.
q-idiom-meaning.eliminate: Other idioms' meanings are usually the wrong options; if you recognise one of them as belonging to a different idiom, cross it out.
traps: The literal meaning is nearly always listed as bait.
The meaning of a similar-sounding idiom is the second common trap.
Do not pick an option only because it contains a word from the idiom.

q-idiom-identify.cue: The full meaning is spelled out in a sentence; the four options are themselves idioms, and you must name the one that carries that meaning.
q-idiom-identify.standard: Decide the feeling the given meaning carries (eager, secretive, angry, lucky), then pick the one option among the four idioms that matches that feeling exactly.
q-idiom-identify.fast: Recall the idiom as a fixed phrase first; do not reason from the individual words of the options.
q-idiom-identify.eliminate: Drop any option idiom whose stored meaning you know is different, even if it shares a word (bell, blood) with the given meaning.
traps: An option that shares a word with the meaning but is a different idiom entirely.
Two idioms built on the same image (bell, water, moon) tested against each other.

pyqs.text: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: At sixes and sevens
options: A dilemma between two evils
A free and fair decision
In complete confusion
A selection made under duress
pyqs.why: At sixes and sevens describes disorder or confusion, as when nobody knows who is doing what.

a.note: A choice between two evils is a dilemma ('between a rock and a hard place'), not confusion; the numbers six and seven tempt one to think of 'two'.

b.note: A free and fair decision is about choice, not disorder.

d.note: A forced selection is about pressure, not about things being in a muddle.

pyqs.trick: Think 'a mess': sixes and sevens is a muddle, never a choice.

pyqs.text: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: Leave no stone unturned
options: To keep shifting from one place to another repeatedly
To make every possible effort to achieve a goal
To remain quiet as a form of protest
To obey someone without questioning
pyqs.why: To leave no stone unturned is to search or try in every way, so that nothing is missed.

a.note: This reads 'stone' and 'turning' as movement; the idiom is about completeness of effort, not travel.

c.note: Staying quiet in protest has no link to effort or searching.

d.note: Obeying without questioning is about submission, not effort.

pyqs.trick: 'No stone left' means everything was tried: effort, not travel.

pyqs.text: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: Blow a fuse
options: To slip away quietly
To vanish suddenly
To become suddenly angry
To manage a situation smartly
pyqs.why: When a fuse blows, the circuit breaks suddenly; the idiom means losing one's temper all at once.

a.note: Slipping away quietly is the opposite of the loud outburst a blown fuse suggests.

b.note: Vanishing suddenly takes 'blow' to mean 'disappear'; a blown fuse is an outburst, not a disappearance.

d.note: Managing a situation smartly has nothing to do with losing control.

pyqs.trick: A blown fuse is an electrical outburst: sudden anger.

pyqs.text: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: Give one the slip
options: to flatter others
to neglect someone
to give a notice
to escape from someone
pyqs.why: To give someone the slip means to escape or get away from them, often by a trick.

a.note: Flattering someone is about praise, unrelated to escaping.

b.note: Neglecting someone is about ignoring a duty, not getting away from a pursuer.

c.note: Giving a notice means a formal warning, which has nothing to do with escape.

pyqs.trick: 'Slip' suggests slipping away unnoticed: to escape.

pyqs.text: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: A red letter day
options: Memorable day
Rose day
Holiday
Birthday
pyqs.why: A red letter day is a memorable day because of some important or pleasant event, not necessarily a holiday or birthday.

b.note: 'Rose day' is not a recognised meaning of this idiom.

c.note: A holiday is a day off work, but a red letter day is defined by being memorable, not by being a holiday.

d.note: A birthday is one kind of memorable day, but the idiom is broader and covers any important or pleasant occasion.

pyqs.trick: Red letters once marked feast days and holy days on old calendars: a day worth remembering.

pyqs.text: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: Up to the minute
options: At the last possible instant or opportunity
To wait or pause
To be as current as is possible
At a very rapid pace
pyqs.why: Up to the minute means as current or up to date as possible, so the sense is about currency of information, not speed or timing.

a.note: 'At the last possible instant' is about timing, confusing 'minute' as a point in time rather than up-to-dateness.

b.note: 'To wait or pause' has no connection to being current.

d.note: 'At a very rapid pace' again reads 'minute' as a unit of speed, not of how current the information is.

pyqs.text: Which of the following idioms has the meaning: 'Eagerly, with great enthusiasm, or ready to enjoy oneself'?
options: Bear the bell
Passing bells
With bells on
Sound as a bell
pyqs.why: 'With bells on' means to come eagerly and enthusiastically, ready to enjoy oneself, exactly the meaning given.

a.note: 'Bear the bell' means to take the lead or be the best at something, not to arrive eagerly.

b.note: 'Passing bells' are the bells rung to mark a death, unrelated to eagerness or enthusiasm.

d.note: 'Sound as a bell' means perfectly healthy or in excellent condition, not eager or enthusiastic.

pyqs.text: Which of the following idioms has the meaning: 'To take advantage of a set of rules, procedures, or structures to achieve a personal or institutional goal, often in a way that is clever, slightly dishonest, or exploits loopholes'?
options: Buck the system
Get something out of one's system
Get something out of your system
Work the system
pyqs.why: 'Work the system' is exactly to take advantage of a set of rules or procedures to achieve a personal or institutional goal, often by exploiting a loophole.

a.note: 'Buck the system' means to resist or go against established rules, the opposite of exploiting them.

b.note: 'Get something out of one's system' means to stop feeling or thinking about something by expressing it, unrelated to rules or procedures.

c.note: 'Get something out of your system' is the same idiom as (b) with a different pronoun, still unrelated to exploiting rules.

pyqs.text: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: Bang for your buck
options: To begin to put forth more effort in some area
To be very healthy
To make money quickly and/or without effort, often through dishonest, unscrupulous, or ethically dubious means
Greater value for the amount of money one is spending
pyqs.why: 'A bigger bang for one's buck' means getting greater value for the money being spent.

a.note: Putting forth more effort is unrelated to value for money.

b.note: Being very healthy has no connection to spending money.

c.note: Making money dishonestly or without effort describes a different idiom ('easy money'), not getting good value for what one spends.
